impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a trial court must defer to the terms of an existing license agreement when assessing copyright infringement damages, and what constitutes a legally permissible use of the 'book of wisdom' in calculating such damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the trial court's use of a hypothetical negotiation to assess copyright infringement damages rather than deferring to an existing license agreement, but vacated the damages award in part because the trial court adopted a legally impermissible view of the 'book of wisdom' doctrine and assessed non-compensatory damages against the government. The case involved the government's unauthorized copying of copyrighted TETRA® software used in military healthcare data interoperability.
impacts.positiveImplications: Confirms that copyright owners are not limited to existing license terms when seeking infringement damages, potentially allowing for higher recoveries through hypothetical negotiation frameworks.
impacts.negativeImplications: Courts must carefully limit damages to compensatory amounts and properly apply the 'book of wisdom' doctrine, which may constrain damages theories in software copyright cases.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act (DTSA) had expired before Insulet brought suit, and how the discovery rule applies to DTSA claims involving the hiring of former employees with knowledge of trade secrets.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict finding trade secret misappropriation under the DTSA, holding that the statute of limitations had expired before suit was filed. The case involved allegations that EOFlow hired former Insulet employees who shared CAD files and proprietary design information for insulin patch pumps. The court determined Insulet was entitled to judgment as a matter of law on limitations grounds.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from strict enforcement of the DTSA's statute of limitations, providing a firm defense when plaintiffs delay filing suit after discovering potential misappropriation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly upon discovering potential misappropriation or risk losing their DTSA claims entirely, even where substantial evidence of misappropriation exists.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding trade secret damages models and in overturning a jury's breach of contract damages award in a case involving misappropriation of automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's judgment on trade secret damages and remanded for a new trial, finding the lower court improperly excluded two damages models. The court also reversed the district court's judgment on breach of contract damages, reinstating the jury award. The case involved Ford's development of replacement software (PDO) after licensing Versata's automotive configuration software under a Master Subscription and Services Agreement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors benefit from broader acceptance of damages models in trade secret cases and stronger deference to jury verdicts on breach of contract damages.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop replacement software after licensing third-party technology face significant liability exposure under both trade secret misappropriation and breach of contract theories.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court properly applied IPR estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar invalidity grounds that were not raised in a prior IPR petition, and what evidentiary standard applies to determining whether a ground 'reasonably could have [been] raised' in that petition.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed and remanded the district court's application of IPR estoppel against Valve, finding insufficient evidence to estop one invalidity ground and that the court failed to adequately account for hindsight bias in estopping another. The case clarifies the standard for determining what prior art a 'skilled searcher conducting a diligent search' would have found, a critical element of IPR estoppel analysis.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent challengers benefit from a more rigorous standard for IPR estoppel, preserving the ability to raise invalidity defenses in district court that were not included in IPR petitions, particularly when prior art discovery involved hindsight considerations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face reduced ability to use IPR estoppel as a shield against invalidity challenges in district court litigation.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a single-question verdict form covering infringement for multiple patents requires a new trial, and whether asserted patent claims directed to wireless building automation systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments and remanded for a new trial, finding that the verdict form's use of a single infringement question covering all asserted patents was prejudicial error. The court also vacated and remanded for further Alice step-two analysis on one patent while affirming eligibility of two other patents' claims directed to wireless building automation systems.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement that verdict forms separately address infringement for each asserted patent, preventing the risk of generalized infringement findings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting multiple patents face procedural complexity and risk of new trials if verdict forms do not properly segregate infringement inquiries by patent.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a non-provisional patent application can claim priority from a provisional application when the non-provisional corrects an alleged typographical error that broadens the scope of a chemical substituent definition, and whether an intervening public disclosure of a compound within only the broadened scope anticipates the claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment invalidating Enanta's patent covering compounds used in coronavirus treatment, holding that the change from 'C2-C12-alkyl' to 'C1-C12-alkyl' was not a correctable typographical error and thus the patent could not claim priority from the provisional application. Pfizer's intervening disclosure of nirmatrelvir (used in Paxlovid®) therefore anticipated the claims. This decision has major implications for pharmaceutical patent strategy around provisional application drafting.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic drug manufacturers and competitors benefit from strict enforcement of priority requirements, preventing patent holders from retroactively broadening provisional application disclosures to capture competing products.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical companies must exercise extreme precision in provisional application drafting, as even minor errors in chemical definitions may be uncorrectable and result in loss of priority dates and patent invalidation.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the six-year statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for claims against the United States in the Court of Federal Claims is subject to American Pipe tolling based on a prior class action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that the six-year statute of limitations in § 2501 is not subject to American Pipe tolling, affirming dismissal of breach of contract and Fifth Amendment taking claims brought by a bank holding company that lost assets during the 2008 financial crisis after investing Tier 1 Capital in Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac preferred shares. The court recognized that its prior decision in Bright v. United States was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's ANZ Securities decision.
impacts.positiveImplications: The government benefits from certainty that the § 2501 limitations period cannot be extended through class action tolling, reducing exposure to stale claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Financial institutions and other businesses with claims against the government must independently file suit within the six-year limitations period and cannot rely on the pendency of a related class action to toll the deadline.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner who retains the right to sue for infringement under a license agreement that grants exclusive rights to a licensee has sufficient constitutional standing to bring an infringement suit against third parties.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who grants an exclusive license but retains the right to sue third parties for infringement possesses an exclusionary right sufficient to satisfy the irreducible constitutional minimum of standing. The court found this retained right was not rendered illusory by the rights granted to the licensee under the agreement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners can structure license agreements to retain enforcement rights while granting exclusive commercial licenses, preserving their ability to independently pursue infringement actions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers may face suits from both licensees and patent owners depending on license structures, potentially increasing litigation exposure.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a relay device for tracking farming operations using GPS, message bus data, and implement profiles are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in declining to find the case exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's asserted claims directed to automated farming data capture and processing were patent-ineligible under § 101, but vacated the district court's refusal to find the case exceptional and remanded for reconsideration of attorney's fees. The decision reinforces the difficulty of patenting data collection and processing systems in agriculture technology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies defending against patent assertions benefit from continued rigorous application of § 101 eligibility standards to data collection and processing claims, and may recover fees when cases are found exceptional.
impacts.negativeImplications: AgTech companies and other businesses seeking to patent data collection, processing, and sharing systems face significant § 101 eligibility barriers, and asserting such patents aggressively may expose them to exceptional case fee awards.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the claim terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in a weight-to-weight ratio limitation, and whether waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal was permissible in a pharmaceutical patent preliminary injunction.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction barring Hetero from launching a generic competitor to Nuedexta, a neurological disorder drug, agreeing with the district court's claim construction. However, the court vacated the waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal, holding that the equities did not support complete waiver. The patent expires in August 2026, making the injunction commercially decisive.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from affirmation of preliminary injunctions blocking generic entry, preserving market exclusivity through patent expiration. The bond requirement vacatur provides some protection for generics.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug manufacturers face barriers to market entry when preliminary injunctions are upheld, though the requirement for bonds pending appeal provides some financial protection against wrongful injunctions.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and how eligibility analysis applies differently to method claims versus system claims implementing the same technology.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of eligibility for certain method claims related to non-uniform constellations used in digital broadcast communications while affirming eligibility for system claims, creating a split outcome based on claim type. The court affirmed the jury's infringement and damages findings against LG. This case has significant implications for the consumer electronics and broadcasting industries.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies benefit from the affirmation that system claims implementing improved communication standards can survive § 101 challenges, and the court's deference to jury damages findings strengthens patent enforcement.
impacts.negativeImplications: The vacatur on method claim eligibility introduces uncertainty for patent holders whose portfolios include both method and system claims directed to the same technology.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a non-party to district court litigation may file an IPR petition on the filing deadline of a party to that litigation, and whether the PTAB's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness determination invalidating claims of FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded for further proceedings. The case involved Qualcomm filing IPR petitions challenging patents asserted by FedEx against Roambee on Roambee's IPR filing deadline, despite Qualcomm not being a party to the underlying litigation. The decision addresses important questions about third-party IPR petitions and their relationship to ongoing litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from closer scrutiny of third-party IPR petitions that appear coordinated with litigation parties, and from the court's willingness to vacate insufficiently supported obviousness determinations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies seeking to use third-party IPR filings as a strategic tool face increased risk that such petitions and resulting PTAB decisions will receive heightened judicial scrutiny.

impacts.caseName: KG Dongbu Steel Co., Ltd. v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Court of International Trade erred in sustaining Commerce's under-protest determination that debt-to-equity conversions conferred no countervailable benefit, and whether Commerce's original equityworthiness determinations should be reinstated.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade and ordered reinstatement of Commerce's original determinations that three debt-to-equity conversions by a Korean steel company conferred countervailable benefits. The decision clarifies Commerce's methodology for evaluating whether government-directed equity infusions in foreign companies constitute unfair subsidies subject to countervailing duties, with direct implications for international steel trade.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic steel manufacturers and other industries competing with subsidized imports benefit from stronger enforcement of countervailing duty laws and deference to Commerce's original equityworthiness determinations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign manufacturers and importers face increased exposure to countervailing duties when their governments have participated in debt-to-equity conversions, even where subsequent Commerce analyses found no benefit.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether doctrine of equivalents infringement was properly barred.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed non-infringement of Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents, agreeing that 'a pH of 13 or higher' refers to pH measured at a temperature standard in the field (25°C) and that Actelion was barred from asserting infringement by equivalents. The decision is significant for pharmaceutical patent claiming practices regarding pH-dependent formulations, as temperature affects pH measurements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies benefit from precise claim construction of pH-related limitations, enabling them to design around branded drug patents based on measurement conditions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical patent holders with claims specifying pH levels face the risk that standard measurement conditions will be read into their claims, potentially narrowing claim scope and enabling non-infringement findings.

impacts.caseName: mCom IP, LLC v. City National Bank of Florida
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether surviving patent claims can be dismissed for obviousness on the same grounds used to invalidate other claims in a completed IPR, and whether such a case qualifies as 'exceptional' for attorney's fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed dismissal of a patent infringement complaint asserting surviving IPR claims of a unified electronic banking patent, finding the claims invalid on the same obviousness grounds that invalidated other claims in the IPR. However, the court reversed the exceptional case finding and fee award under § 285 and the attorney sanction under § 1927, holding that the grounds were insufficient to support either finding.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants benefit from the ability to challenge surviving IPR claims on the same invalidity grounds used against other claims of the same patent. The reversal of fee awards also limits the deterrent effect on patent assertion.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders whose claims survive IPR face the risk of district court invalidation on the same grounds applied to canceled claims, though the reversal of fee sanctions provides some comfort for asserting patents in good faith.
